intro: “Hasche-Mann” (Blind Man’s Buff), No. 3 of Kinderszenen, Op. 15, is a game of chase in B minor. Sharp cries cut across its running semiquavers.

sections.label: B · Passage towards G
sections.mNote: A slurred passage interrupts the running notes.

cues.title: Opening, bars 1–8
cues.text: Each short phrase begins sforzando-piano, a sharp accent followed at once by a soft dynamic. The semiquavers run up and down under staccato dots. The left hand plays short chords and descending semiquaver runs of its own.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, plate 6016, p. 6, bars 1–8. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/fe/IMSLP03060-Schumann-Op015Brt6016.pdf
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Second part, bars 9–20
cues.text: The second part carries the same running figure onto G–B–D harmony at bar 9. In the slurred bars 13–16 the upper notes are held while the left hand climbs by semitones into bar 17. The opening chase then starts again.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 6, bars 9–20; G–B–D at bar 9, slurred writing in bars 13–16 and chromatic ascent into bar 17.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Marie Wieck’s concert, 1853
cues.text: On 18 January 1853 Marie Wieck, Clara’s younger half-sister, played six of the Kinderszenen. She placed Schumann’s third piece last on the programme.
cues.evidence: Thomas Synofzik, 175 Jahre Kinderszenen (2013), item 15, reproducing Marie Wieck’s concert programme. https://www.schumann-zwickau.de/media/archiv-sonderausstellungen/2013_175_Jahre_Kinderszenen.pdf

transitions.title: The same phrase in G major
transitions.how: The B minor phrase ends on B. The next outburst keeps B in the bass and places G above it, moving to G major harmony. The sforzando-piano attack and the staccato semiquavers continue across the double bar without a break.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel first edition, p. 6, bars 8–9; bass and chord pitches confirmed in Ying-Chun Liu’s Mutopia transcription, based on Leichte Stücke (1900).

composer.epithet: Composer and music critic, a bookseller’s son, whose piano music depicts lovers, masks and arguments.
facts: Friedrich Wieck, piano; Heinrich Dorn, composition
Co-founded the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik in 1834; edited it until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
composer.background:
Robert Schumann grew up among books in Zwickau. His father August sold and published them, and encouraged his son’s music; Robert read Jean Paul’s novels while learning the piano. The novels contain twins, disguises, and conversations that wander from their subject and return to it unexpectedly. In Papillons, his early set of piano dances, Schumann took up the masked ball at the end of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre.

He went to Leipzig to study law in 1828 and moved to Heidelberg the following year. In the end he persuaded his mother to let him pursue music. Friedrich Wieck undertook to train him as a pianist. Wieck’s young daughter Clara was already performing in public; Robert was the older pupil and had more ground to make up. By 1832 paralysis in his right hand had ended his hopes of becoming a virtuoso. He studied composition with Heinrich Dorn and turned to composing and writing.
